summary.text: Taking \(m=39101\), let \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\); modular exponentiation and gcd computations in \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)[\sqrt{41}]\) show that, for every prime divisor \(p\mid N\), a fixed element has exact order \(N+1\), using the prime divisors \(2,3,100943\) of \(N+1\). If \(N\) were composite, its least prime divisor would satisfy \(p^2\le N\), but this algebra has only \(p^2\) elements and hence cannot contain an element of order \(N+1>p^2\); thus \(N\) is prime, providing the required positive-step witness.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 N=2\cdot 100943\cdot 3^{39101}-1
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 M=N+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}.
\]
We will prove that \(N\) is prime. Since \(39101>0\), this will give a positive index \(m=39101\) for which
\[
2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1
\]
is prime, and hence will disprove the assertion that \(a(100943)=0\).

The primality proof uses an order certificate in a quadratic algebra. The point of using a quadratic algebra rather than just the ordinary residue ring is that, for a prime divisor \(p\) of \(N\), the algebra has exactly \(p^2\) elements. We will exhibit an element whose order would have to be \(N+1\). If \(N\) were composite and \(p\) were its least prime divisor, then \(p^2\leq N\), contradicting the existence of an element of order \(N+1\) in a set with only \(p^2\) elements.

For any positive integer \(n\), define
\[
 R_n=(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)[u]/(u^2-41).
\]
Thus an element is represented by a pair \((x,y)\), standing for \(x+yu\), and multiplication is
\[
 (x,y)(z,w)=(xz+41yw,\;xw+yz)\pmod n.
\]
The identity is \((1,0)\). In particular, if \(p\) is prime, then \(R_p\) has exactly \(p^2\) elements, regardless of whether \(u^2-41\) is irreducible modulo \(p\).

We use the following element of \(R_N\):
\[
 \gamma=-\frac{21}{20}-\frac1{20}u.
\]
The denominator is legitimate modulo \(N\). Indeed, \(N\) is odd, and modulo \(5\) we have
\[
3^{39101}\equiv3\pmod5,
\]
because \(39101\equiv1\pmod4\), while \(100943\equiv3\pmod5\). Hence
\[
N\equiv 2\cdot3\cdot3-1\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
Thus \(\gcd(20,N)=1\), so \(20\) has an inverse modulo \(N\). Notice also that
\[
\left(-\frac{21}{20}\right)^2-41\left(-\frac1{20}\right)^2
 =\frac{441-41}{400}=1,
\]
so \(\gamma\) has norm \(1\), although the order argument below needs the explicit power computations rather than merely this norm identity.

Here is the finite modular computation forming the certificate. It can be performed entirely with integer arithmetic as follows. To compute \(\gamma^e\), write \(e\) in binary, begin with \((1,0)\), and read the binary digits from most significant to least significant. At each digit, square the current pair using
\[
(x,y)^2=(x^2+41y^2,\;2xy)\pmod N,
\]
and, when the digit is \(1\), multiply the result by
\[
\gamma=\left(-21\cdot20^{-1},-20^{-1}\right)

after reduction modulo \(N\). Reducing both coordinates modulo \(N\) after every multiplication gives the following results:
\[
\gamma^{M/2}=(-1,0),                                      \tag{1}
\]
\[
\gamma^{M/3}=\left(\frac{N-1}{2},s_3\right)              \tag{2}
\]
for a certain residue \(s_3\), and, writing
\[
\gamma^{M/100943}=(r_q,s_q),                              \tag{3}
\]
the Euclidean algorithm gives
\[
\gcd(r_q-1,N)=1.                                          \tag{4}
\]
Here \(r_q-1\) in (4) may equivalently be replaced by its least nonnegative residue modulo \(N\). Equations (1)--(3) are obtained by the binary square-and-multiply recurrence just described; (4) is the ensuing ordinary integer gcd computation. Thus no probable-prime assumption is involved in these relations: their mathematical content is a finite chain of pair multiplications and Euclidean divisions.

For completeness, the other two nonidentity gcd conditions can be read off without retaining any large terminal coordinates. From (1), the real coordinate minus \(1\) is \(-2\), and hence
\[
\gcd((-1)-1,N)=\gcd(2,N)=1,                              \tag{5}
\]
since \(N\) is odd. From (2), the real coordinate minus \(1\) is \((N-3)/2\). Also \(N\equiv-1\pmod3\), because the term \(2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}\) is divisible by \(3\). Therefore \(3\nmid N\). Any common divisor of \((N-3)/2\) and \(N\) divides both \(N\) and \(N-3\), and hence divides \(3\); since it cannot be \(3\), it is \(1\). Consequently
\[
\gcd\left(\frac{N-3}{2},N\right)=1.                     \tag{6}
\]
Finally, squaring (1) gives
\[
\gamma^M=(1,0).                                           \tag{7}
\]

We now explain why these computations prove that \(N\) is prime. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(N\) is composite, and let \(p\) be its least prime divisor. Since \(N>1\), such a \(p\) exists. The standard least-prime-factor argument gives
\[
p^2\leq N:                                                \tag{8}
\]
indeed, writing \(N=pk\), if \(k<p\), then a prime divisor of \(k\) would be a prime divisor of \(N\) smaller than \(p\); hence \(k\geq p\).

Reduce the coordinates of \(\gamma\) and all the displayed power identities modulo \(p\). This is valid because \(p\mid N\): every congruence modulo \(N\) is also a congruence modulo \(p\). Let \(g\in R_p\) be the resulting element. Equation (7) yields
\[
g^M=1.                                                    \tag{9}
\]
On the other hand, none of the following three powers is \(1\):
\[
g^{M/2}\ne1,\qquad g^{M/3}\ne1,\qquad
 g^{M/100943}\ne1.                                       \tag{10}
\]
To justify this uniformly, suppose one of the powers were \(1=(1,0)\) in \(R_p\). Its real coordinate would then be congruent to \(1\pmod p\). But the corresponding real coordinate minus \(1\) is relatively prime to \(N\), by (5), (6), or (4), whereas \(p\mid N\). It therefore cannot be divisible by \(p\), a contradiction.

We next determine the prime divisors of \(M\). A direct trial division through \(\sqrt{100943}<318\) shows that \(100943\) is prime: division by each prime at most \(317\) leaves a nonzero remainder. Therefore, from
\[
M=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101},
\]
the only prime divisors of \(M\) are
\[
2,\quad3,\quad100943.                                    \tag{11}
\]

Let \(d\) be the multiplicative order of \(g\). Equation (9) implies that \(d\mid M\). We claim that in fact \(d=M\). If \(d<M\), then \(M/d>1\), so some prime \(q\) divides \(M/d\). Thus \(q\mid M\) and \(d\mid M/q\), which would imply
\[
g^{M/q}=1.
\]
By (11), \(q\) must be \(2\), \(3\), or \(100943\), and every one of these possibilities contradicts (10). Hence
\[
\operatorname{ord}(g)=M=N+1.                              \tag{12}
\]

The powers of one element form \(\operatorname{ord}(g)\) distinct elements of \(R_p\). Since \(R_p\) has exactly \(p^2\) elements, (12) gives
\[
N+1=M\leq p^2.                                            \tag{13}
\]
But (8) says \(p^2\leq N\). Combining the inequalities gives
\[
N+1\leq p^2\leq N,
\]
which is impossible. This contradiction proves that
\[
N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime.

It remains to translate this into the sequence statement. For \(n=100943\), let
\[
S=\{m\in\mathbb N:m\geq1\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^m-1
\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
We have shown that \(39101\in S\). Thus \(S\) is nonempty, and every member of \(S\) is positive. Its least member therefore exists and is positive. By the definition of A354747, that least member is \(a(100943)\). Consequently
\[
a(100943)>0,
\]
and in particular
\[
a(100943)\ne0.
\]
Thus the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\) is false.
